title: Habitat for Humanity’s Next 50 Years: Leadership Lessons from the 2026 Affiliate Conference
summary: Explore leadership lessons from the 2026 Habitat for Humanity Affiliate Conference on innovation, organizational resilience, and Habitat's next 50 years.
body_markdown:
*At Habitat’s 50-year milestone, leaders in Atlanta explored a question that reaches well beyond homebuilding: how do you keep a mission steady while changing the way you work?*


At the[2026 Habitat for Humanity International Affiliate Conference](https://web.cvent.com/event/7a737e06-1da4-42b1-9a1f-61efc3ff9b06/websitePage:46c79c03-caaa-4beb-97de-a4e79734d657?RefId=Agenda) , the conversation was about more than celebrating five decades of impact. During the October 8 general session, speakers considered what it will take for affiliates to meet changing housing needs, make room for new ideas, and build organizations strong enough for the work ahead.


Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph joined Habitat leaders Dwayne Spencer and Sabrina Lippman in approaching that challenge from different angles. Their experiences pointed to a shared idea: commitment to a mission does not require commitment to every old way of doing things.


## **How Can Habitat Affiliates Innovate Without Taking Big Risks?**


Marc Randolph’s keynote began with the early days of Netflix, when the company was still searching for a model that could survive. He described the willingness to test ideas, discover what was not working, and make difficult changes rather than defend a familiar approach.


His advice was not that every organization should chase a dramatic reinvention. Small experiments matter.


For a Habitat affiliate, that could mean testing a different volunteer check-in process, trying a new way to communicate with prospective partners, or simplifying one step in the homebuyer journey.


The useful question is not whether an idea will definitely work. It’s what an organization could try on a manageable scale, and what it might learn in the process.


When staff time and budgets are tight, that distinction matters.


## **What Does It Mean to Respond to a Community’s Changing Needs?**


Dwayne Spencer, CEO of Habitat for Humanity of Greater Memphis, reflected on how his view of Habitat’s work has expanded over 25 years.


Building homes remains central, but the needs surrounding housing are broader. His remarks touched on aging in place, health, neighborhood investment, and advocacy.


That perspective invites a question every affiliate can ask:


**What does our community need from us now?**


The answer will differ by geography, housing market, and the people an affiliate serves. A strategy that makes sense in Memphis may not be right for a smaller rural affiliate.


For nonprofit leaders outside Habitat, the principle is familiar. Listening closely to the community sometimes reveals that the mission is constant, even when the most useful response changes.


## **Why Do Strong Internal Operations Matter to Habitat’s Future?**


Sabrina Lippman, CEO of Habitat for Humanity New York City and Westchester, spoke about the need to build organizations that can sustain their commitments.


That includes healthy finances, strong teams, community trust, and partnerships, alongside the long-term work of keeping housing affordable.


Those subjects may sound less urgent than the next construction milestone. But they shape whether an affiliate can deliver consistently over time.


If staff responsibilities are unclear or the organization has taken on more than its team can support, even a promising new initiative can become difficult to sustain.


Taking care of the organization is not separate from taking care of the mission. It’s part of the same responsibility.


## **What Should Nonprofit Leaders Consider Stopping?**


One of the most practical ideas in the session was that moving forward does not always mean adding something.


Lippman also encouraged leaders to consider what they may need to stop doing.


That’s a hard question in organizations where people are accustomed to stretching to meet every need. Yet each new project competes for staff attention, funding, and leadership time.


An established process may deserve a fresh look. A partnership may make more sense than managing an activity alone.


Choosing what to set aside can be just as deliberate, and just as mission-driven, as deciding what to pursue.


## **How Can Leaders Put Conference Ideas Into Practice?**


The challenge with any conference is what happens after everyone gets home.


There are inboxes to clear, homes to build, volunteers to coordinate, and immediate decisions waiting.


Randolph urged attendees to act on ideas rather than spend too long debating them.


For an affiliate, that might mean choosing one experiment to run this quarter, bringing one difficult question to the board, or[asking staff where a process creates unnecessary work](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/all-in-one-nonprofit-crm/) .


Habitat’s first 50 years offer plenty to celebrate. The next chapter will ask affiliates to respond to different community needs while preserving what has always made the mission matter: people coming together around decent, affordable housing.


At Giveffect, we value opportunities to learn from Habitat leaders and the practical conversations that happen when[affiliates share what they are trying](https://www.giveffect.com/nonprofit-resource-center/habitat-for-humanity-laramie-county-case-study/) .


The strongest ideas from this conference are not just worth discussing. They’re worth bringing home.
